1.pericope_label: Open thy doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour thy cedars. Howl, fir tree; for the cedar is fallen
debates: Whether Lebanon means the temple, the land, or the mountain itself
Which destruction of the city is foretold
Whether the trees stand for men or for what was built from them
outliers: Henry reports a tradition that the temple gates opened of themselves forty years before its fall, and a rabbi who read this verse by it
Calvin explains why a book of promises turns to threatening, and gives three reasons for the change of strain
Wesley alone keeps the shepherds and lions literal where the others make them rulers
themes: Doors that would not open for a king and must open for a fire
Two crooks broken and worse instruments taken up
Promises that harden the hypocrite unless a threat follows
Lions that ranged the thickets of a river bank

4.pericope_label: Thus saith the LORD my God; Feed the flock of the slaughter; whose possessors slay them, and hold themselves not guilty
debates: Who the possessors that slay the flock are
Whether the threat falls on one land or on the world
Which conqueror is meant by the hand the people are given into
outliers: Gill expressly rejects the foreign conquerors and lays the slaughter on the people own religious teachers
Ellicott reads land as world and men as mankind, turning a local threat into a general one
Clarke names an earlier empire where Gill and Wesley name a later one
themes: A flock fattened for the knife and told it is being fed
Teachers who ruin souls and think it a service
Thanks given to God for the profits of oppression
Two staves named Favour and Bands

7.pericope_label: And I will feed the flock of slaughter, even you, O poor of the flock. And I took unto me two staves; the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Bands
debates: Whether the staves are working crooks or tokens of favour and reunion
Who the three shepherds cut off in one month are
Whether the month is a literal month or a symbolic period
outliers: Clarke assigns each crook a shepherd use, one for marking the tithe and one for catching sheep by the leg
Gill lists and rejects five identifications of the three shepherds before offering his own
Ellicott rejects a scheme that makes a prophetic day worth seven years, on the ground that no instance of it can be cited
themes: A crook dipped in red to mark every tenth sheep
Two houses bound in brotherhood for the first time since they parted
Three men, or three offices, or three empires
A shepherd who stops feeding but has not yet left

10.pericope_label: And I took my staff, even Beauty, and cut it asunder, that I might break my covenant which I had made with all the people
debates: What the broken staff stands for, and whose covenant is annulled
Whether the money goes to a potter or to the treasury
Whether the breach of brotherhood requires the northern kingdom to be still standing
outliers: Ellicott reports that one letter separates the potter from the treasury in the old Greek, and thinks the phrase was proverbial for throwing something away
Gill distinguishes three moments at which the covenant was broken, in right, in appearance, and in fact
Clarke reports a writer who cannot explain the second staff at all on a late date for the prophecy
themes: A gospel that cannot fail but can move house
Wages asked as a test of gratitude
The price of a slave weighed out for a shepherd
A divorce pronounced where the covenant was ratified

15.pericope_label: And the LORD said unto me, Take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd
debates: Whether the foolish shepherd instruments differ from a good shepherd at all
Who the foolish shepherd is, one man or a class
Whether a passage from a later chapter belongs at the end of this one
outliers: Clarke describes each implement as defective where Ellicott says it is needless to ask whether they differ
Gill lists and rejects seven identifications of the foolish shepherd before reporting one he leaves standing
Ellicott reports a proposed transposition of text and finds apparently some truth in it
themes: A bag without bread and a staff without a hook
A yoke made heavier by tradition than the law made it
A withered arm for the workman who would not work
A blinded eye for the watchman who slept
